state.case_summary:
A 74-year-old female with a history of severe aortic stenosis and interventricular septal hypertrophy underwent bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement along with septal myectomy. Two months after the surgery, she experienced syncope and was admitted to another hospital. At presentation, the patient, who is obese, had a heart rate of 40 beats per minute and stable blood pressure. There was no jugular venous distention, but occasional cannon A waves were observed. Lung examination showed adequate aeration in all fields without crackles or wheezing. The point of maximum impulse was not displaced. Heart sounds were regular with variable intensity, without atrial or ventricular gallops, but an early systolic murmur grade II/VI was noted at the left sternal border. Due to symptomatic bradycardia, a dual chamber pacemaker was recommended and successfully implanted. The patient was discharged 24 hours after the procedure. Four months later, during a follow-up visit, she reported no complaints and was doing well. An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular systolic function and proper functioning of the prosthetic aortic valve, with no other abnormalities.

An echocardiogram obtained at the time of her initial visit, while still asymptomatic, showed normal left ventricular chamber dimensions, systolic function, and bioprosthetic valve function. In addition, a pacer wire that was correctly positioned in the right ventricular apex was also seen. However, an abnormal color flow signal arising from the interventricular septum with a predominant flow away from the transducer into the left ventricular cavity was noted. Continuous and pulse wave Doppler interrogation demonstrated a continuous flow with a predominant diastolic component. This abnormal color flow signal, traversing the interventricular septum, was never identified in previous studies.
